title: The Mega Plaza
pageTitle: Apply Area Concepts to Solve Problems

intro.caption: Lesson 5-4 — area of composite figures. The town's new Mega Plaza is an L-shaped stone deck with a fountain hole and a regular hexagon garden. Three gates and a paving budget boss stand between the crew and opening day.

balloons.t: No single formula fits this whole plaza! We have to decompose it into simple shapes.
Blurb! I decomposed the map into three bites.
Split the L into two rectangles that do NOT overlap, then add their areas.
Oops—I used the corner twice! No wonder my number was too big.

pages.caption: To find a composite figure's area, break it into rectangles or triangles with no overlap.

balloons.t: Find each rectangle's area cleanly, then add them together!
No stone goes inside the fountain! Find the big rectangle, then subtract the cutout.
Blurb! Fountain space belongs to me!
A regular hexagon splits from the center into 6 identical triangles!
Find one triangle's area with ½ × b × h, then multiply by 6.
We just added all the outside edge lengths and multiplied by 2 gold!
That's perimeter, not area! Let's price the real square blocks.
140 stone blocks, 168 garden blocks, and zero wasted gold!

win.caption: Decompose composite figures into simple shapes: add joined pieces, subtract cutouts, and split regular polygons into congruent triangles.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Split the Figure
gates.prompt: Find the area of the L-shaped patio made of a 12 × 5 rectangle and a 6 × 4 rectangle.
hints: Conceptual: decomposing means breaking a shape into pieces that fit together without overlapping.
Procedural: multiply length × width for each rectangle, then add the two areas.

steps: Practice L-shape: a 10 × 4 rectangle and a 5 × 6 rectangle (no overlap).
worked.q: An L-shape splits into an 8 × 3 rectangle and a 4 × 5 rectangle. Total area?

items.label: Total area (12 × 5 plus 6 × 4):
items.aria: total area of L-shaped patio in square blocks

fb.msg: 36 is 60 − 24. Both rectangles are part of the patio, so add them.
54 added the perimeters (34 + 20) instead of the areas.

items.q: Dree tried 12 × 5 = 60 and 6 × 9 = 54 by using the full height 9 twice. What went wrong?

options.t: She subtracted a hole that wasn't there
options.fb: She added both rectangles, so nothing was subtracted.

options.t: She multiplied by ½ by mistake
options.fb: There is no ½ in 12 × 5 or 6 × 9.

gates.pass: Eighty-four square blocks, zero overlap! Dree puts the duplicate tiles away.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Subtract the Hole
gates.prompt: The main deck is 16 by 10 blocks with a 5 by 4 fountain cutout in the middle.
hints: Conceptual: when a hole or cutout is removed from a shape, subtract its area from the outer shape.
Procedural: find 16 × 10 for the full deck, find 5 × 4 for the fountain, then subtract.

steps: Practice deck: 15 × 8 outer rectangle with a 4 × 5 cutout.
worked.q: A 11 × 6 deck has a 3 × 4 cutout. What is the remaining area?

items.label: Deck area (16 × 10 minus 5 × 4 fountain):
items.aria: remaining deck area in square blocks

fb.msg: 180 added the fountain (160 + 20) instead of subtracting the cutout.
160 is the whole rectangle before subtracting the 5 × 4 fountain hole.

items.fbDefault: Subtract the 5 × 4 fountain area from the 16 × 10 deck area.

items.q: When do you subtract areas in a composite figure?

options.t: Whenever two shapes are placed side by side
options.fb: Side-by-side shapes are joined together, so you add their areas.

options.t: When a piece or cutout is removed from a larger shape
Whenever a figure has a triangle
options.fb: Triangles can be added or subtracted depending on whether they are part of the shape or cut out.

gates.pass: 140 square blocks of stone deck, and Gel keeps his splash zone!

gates.title: Gate 3 · Hexagon into Triangles
gates.prompt: Moss's regular hexagon garden splits into 6 congruent triangles. Each triangle has base 8 and height 7.
hints: Conceptual: a regular polygon splits from its center into congruent triangles—one for each side.
Procedural: find one triangle's area with ½ × 8 × 7, then multiply by 6.

steps: Practice pentagon: 5 congruent triangles, each with base 4 and height 3.
worked.q: A regular octagon splits into 8 triangles, each with area 5. Total area?

items.label: Area of ONE triangle (b = 8, h = 7):
items.aria: area of one triangle in the hexagon garden

fb.msg: 56 is 8 × 7 without the ½. A triangle is half of a rectangle.

items.label: Total area of the 6-triangle hexagon:
items.aria: total area of the regular hexagon garden

fb.msg: 336 is 6 × 56 — you forgot the ½ in each triangle!
28 is just one triangle. Multiply by 6 for the whole hexagon.

gates.pass: 28 per triangle, 168 square blocks total for the flower garden!

gates.title: Boss Gate · Cost the Plaza
gates.prompt: Combine the 140-square-block stone deck and the 168-square-block hexagon garden, then price the whole job at 2 gold per square block.
hints: Conceptual: add the areas of the separate plaza sections, then multiply total area by cost per square block.
Procedural: first add 140 + 168. Then multiply that total by 2 gold.

steps: Practice plaza: 50 square blocks total, at 3 gold per square block.
worked.q: A 60-square-block plaza costs 4 gold per square block. Total cost?

items.label: Lock 1 · Total plaza area (140 + 168):
items.aria: total area of plaza deck and garden

fb.msg: 28 is 168 − 140. Both sections are being built, so add them.

items.label: Lock 2 · Total cost (308 sq blocks × 2 gold):
items.aria: total cost of the plaza in gold

fb.msg: 310 is 308 + 2. Multiply total area by 2 gold per square block.
154 is 308 ÷ 2. Each square block costs 2 gold, so multiply.

items.q: Lock 3 · Why did The Champs' perimeter-adding method fail?

options.t: Perimeter measures the outer border, not the flat surface inside
Perimeter always gives a bigger number than area
options.fb: Sometimes perimeter is smaller and sometimes bigger—the real issue is it measures border length, not surface.

options.t: You have to multiply perimeters instead of adding them
options.fb: Multiplying perimeters still does not measure square units inside the shape.

gates.pass: 308 square blocks, 616 gold! The plaza opens right on budget.

journal.heading: Lesson 5-4 — what the mega plaza taught us
rows: Split composite shapes into non-overlapping rectangles or triangles, then add their areas.
When a hole or cutout is removed, find the outer area and subtract the hole's area.
Split a regular polygon from its center into congruent triangles, find one area, and multiply by the number of sides.
Tiles and flowers cover surface area (square units), not the border length (perimeter).
journal.quote: "No overlapping corners, no missing cutouts, and plenty of room to bounce." — Gel

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 5-4 (Apply Area Concepts to Solve Problems). Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. Covers decomposing composite figures without overlap, subtracting cutouts, splitting regular polygons into congruent triangles, and solving area cost problems.
standards: Derive a formula for the area of a right triangle using a rectangle; find the area of triangles and special quadrilaterals by decomposing or composing
